cultivar: Local Yixing small-leaf population bushes, with introduced cultivars such as Fuding Dabai in newer gardens
processing: Fully oxidised small-leaf black: tender spring buds and young leaves are withered, rolled, oxidised and dried gently, then lightly sorted.
harvest_season: Spring, with the top lots picked before Qingming; the 'Yixing Hong' mark is a spring-only tea.
appearance_dry: Small, tight, slightly curled dark strands with a scattering of golden tips.
appearance_wet: Small, tender copper-red leaves, even and soft.
taste_profile: Mild and honey-sweet with caramel and a light fruitiness, low tannin and a soft, clean finish; a gentle tea rather than a bold one.

brewing.notes: Locals brew it in a zisha pot, which suits its softness; 90 °C and short steeps. Western-style: 3 g per 250 ml, 2.5–3 minutes, neat.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's spring harvest, with pre-Qingming lots at the top, mostly within Jiangsu and through zisha-teapot sellers; drink within a year. There is no vintage market.
description:
Yixing is famous for its purple-clay teapots, and Yixing Hong Cha is the black tea grown alongside them. The town on the shore of Lake Tai in southern Jiangsu has grown tea since at least the Tang dynasty under the old name Yangxian, and its hills are among Jiangsu's main tea districts; black tea has been made there since the late Qing, and since 2018 'Yixing Hong' has been a registered geographical indication mark.

It is made from small-leaf bushes picked in spring, the best before Qingming, then withered, rolled, oxidised and dried gently. The small leaf and gentle finish make it a soft tea: low in tannin, sweet, with none of the malt and muscle of a big-leaf black.

Expect honey and caramel, a light fruit note and a clean, mild finish over five or six short steeps; it is easy to drink and easy to over-steep into blandness rather than bitterness, so keep infusions short. It is often brewed in a small zisha pot, and because a clay pot rounds off edges a tea this soft loses little in one.

It is sold as the current spring, mostly in Jiangsu and from teapot sellers, and it rarely travels abroad. Buy by picking date and look for small, even, tippy leaf with a sweet dry aroma.

If you have just bought a zisha pot, this is an obvious tea to try in it: forgiving, sweet and unlikely to leave a flavour you regret.
history:
Yixing, the old Yangxian, is known for tea far older than its black tea: Yangxian was a tribute tea in the Tang dynasty, praised by Lu Yu and later in verse by Su Dongpo. That fame belongs to the earlier teas of the area.

Black tea here is reported from the Guangxu era of the Qing dynasty. The modern name came much later: Yixing Hong was registered as a geographical indication certification mark in April 2018, and local promotion now presents it as a spring-only tea from buds picked before Qingming. Little has been written on the years between.
